newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU's Van Miert talks tough on Cr Lyonnais.
newsitem.headline: EU's Van Miert talks tough on Cr Lyonnais.

text.p: European Commissioner Karel Van Miert accused Credit Lyonnais of unfair play and said in an interview to be published on Friday he would demand sizeable French asset sell-offs by the bank in new state-aid talks.

But, despite harsh words for the debt-laden bank, Van Miert acknowledged the European Commission would need to keep in mind the affect on the French banking sector generally of his demands further subsidies to the state-owned bank be approved by him.
The Commission approved a big French aid and rescue plan for Credit Lyonnais in July 1995 in return for a promise to sell of assets outside France.
It recently gave clearance for a further emergency aid package and is gearing up for talks on what conditions it will attach to further state aid.

"Over and above the asset sales already demanded outside France, I think it is now inevitable that we require similar and extremely significant measures in France itself," said Van Miert, who is in charge of state aid control in the EU, in an interview in French daily Les Echos.

"We do not intend to draw a line in the past," he said. "When we gave our approval on July 26, 1995 to a sizeable aid package, it was tied to a series of conditions. They have been relaxed temporarily with the grant of emergency aid."

"But I must repeat it, that does not mean -- as I believe I understood from a declaration by (Credit Lyonnais chairman Jean) Peyrelevade -- that we will just paper over the past," the paper quoted him as saying.

"This time round, we'll have to have everything laid out on the table, including all the ghosts in the cupboard...When I say that I am not only expressing disappointment but also a reproach, because Credit Lyonnais did not play the game."
"When you strike a deal you have to stick by it. On this level, Credit Lyonnais did not behave," Van Miert said.

The aid package agreed by the Commission in mid-1995 was the second in two years after the huge state bank, once the largest outside Japan, ran up 21 billion francs of losses between 1992 and 1994 following expansion in the late 1980s that went badly wrong.

But some of the financing terms for that rescue package were pulling the bank back into the red, hence Van Miert's approval of a 3.9 billion francs emergency aid pending the drawing up of yet another rescue which press speculation says could involve a recapitalisation of about 10 billion francs.

Despite the tough words from Van Miert, banking analysts say it is hard to see just how much more can in reality be demanded of Credit Lyonnais if, as the government has promised, it is to be prepared for privatisation before the end of the decade.
